conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that ivermectin does not lower the risk of death in COVID-19, citing large, high-quality randomized controlled trials to reject the claim.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
The evidence indicates the answer is actually **no** — ivermectin does not lower the risk of death in COVID-19.

The largest and most rigorous randomized controlled trials contradict this claim. The TOGETHER trial, described as "the largest randomized, double-blind trial yet conducted" on ivermectin for COVID-19, found no significant reduction in hospitalization or death, showing "nearly parallel lines for ivermectin versus placebo for both hospitalization outcome & for death" (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2115869; reported by https://www.nytimes.com/2022/03/30/health/covid-ivermectin-hospitalization.html). Similarly, ACTIV-6, a large U.S. randomized trial with over 4,000 participants, "found ivermectin was not effective as a COVID-19 treatment" (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ivermectin_during_the_COVID-19_pandemic).

A synthesis of the trial evidence notes that "the higher-quality, larger trials and updated meta-analyses find no convincing benefit on mortality, hospitalization, or major clinical endpoints" (https://factually.co/fact-checks/health/ivermectin-covid-19-randomized-trials-meta-analyses-efficacy-safety-limitations-87d1c4).

While some meta-analyses pooling many smaller, lower-quality studies (e.g., c19early.org) report significant mortality reductions, these aggregations include studies later found to be flawed or fraudulent, and are not considered reliable by mainstream health authorities. The World Health Organization and FDA both state current evidence does not support ivermectin's effectiveness against COVID-19, recommending it only within clinical trials (https://www.drugs.com/ivermectin.html).

**Conclusion:** Based on the largest, most methodologically sound randomized trials, ivermectin does not reduce COVID-19 mortality. The claim that it does is supported mainly by weaker, pooled analyses of lower-quality studies, not by definitive trial evidence.
